standard_prerequisites.name: Set and 1-type
standard_prerequisites.statement: A set is a type whose path types are mere propositions, and a 1-type is a type whose path types are sets.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the two levels related by the statement.

standard_prerequisites.name: Dependent action on paths and transport in a path family
standard_prerequisites.statement: The action on paths of a dependent function yields a dependent path, and transport in a family of paths computes by concatenation.
standard_prerequisites.use: They turn the action on paths into an explicit concatenation identity.

standard_prerequisites.name: Cancellation
standard_prerequisites.statement: A common left factor of an equality can be cancelled.

core_obligations: Assume a proof of set-ness and fix x, y and a path p between them (source line 122).
Define the auxiliary function sending a path q to the set-ness proof applied to x, y, p and q (source lines 122-123).

Apply the dependent action on paths of that function to a path r between two such q and compute the resulting dependent path through the transport rule in a path family to get an explicit concatenation identity (source lines 124-125).
Apply the identity to two paths between p and q and cancel the common factor to conclude that they are equal, which is exactly the statement that the path type is a set (source lines 127-128).

proof_roadmap.step: Set up the auxiliary function from the set-ness proof.
Turn its action on paths into a concatenation identity.
Cancel to get uniqueness of paths between paths.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source lines 117-120 (book Lemma 3.1.8): if a type is a set then it is a 1-type. The statement is a level implication whose verification requires comparing paths between paths, and the proof (source lines 121-128) has to produce that comparison: it fixes a path p, turns the set-ness proof into a dependent function on paths out of p, applies its dependent action on paths to a path r between two such paths, computes the resulting dependent path through the transport rule in a path family into an explicit concatenation identity, and then cancels a common factor to conclude that any two paths between p and q coincide. The cancellation step and the transport computation are the content and neither is visible in the statement.
